title: Purpose
author: Mr. Nickhart
summary: Mr. Nickhart applies the Desmond Tutu upstream/downstream metaphor to school leadership, arguing that when leaders spend disproportionate time quality-assuring classroom outputs (pulling people out of the river), it is because the upstream problem -- the absence of clear, shared purpose -- has not been addressed. Without purpose, leaders can only manage the downstream because there is nothing else to anchor attention. Purpose is not a mission statement but a set of interlocking elements: aims and values, strategic priorities, and the specific curriculum and pedagogical decisions that flow from them. When purpose is well-defined, communicated, and understood, colleagues know what to prioritize in the limited time they have to influence what children learn -- and quality assurance becomes an upstream investment rather than downstream firefighting.
points: The Tutu upstream/downstream metaphor distinguishes downstream quality assurance (monitoring what teachers do, scrutinizing books) from upstream investment (defining and communicating the purpose that shapes what teachers prioritize) -- both are necessary, but the ratio matters enormously.

When purpose is absent, leaders' attention defaults entirely to the downstream because there is no upstream substance to anchor it; this is how assessment-driven school cultures emerge -- not from malice but from a vacuum of curriculum substance.

Purpose drives motivation and therefore what colleagues actually do in the short time they have to influence student learning -- getting purpose right has a multiplier effect that monitoring alone cannot achieve.

The historical shift toward high-stakes testing, lesson observations, and work scrutinies was a symptom: without well-developed curriculum knowledge upstream, checking and judging became the only available lever.

Improving school quality requires not just better monitoring tools but a clarity of purpose that makes monitoring more targeted, more upstream, and more meaningful -- scrutinizing purpose so people stop falling in the river in the first place.
quotes: There is a good chance that, when we look at things going on at department or classroom level and are not happy with what we find, we are seeing the symptoms of a problem further upstream, rather than the cause of the problem.
There comes a point where we need to stop just pulling people out of the river. We need to go upstream and find out why they're falling in.

I have a hypothesis around the establishment of the checking and judging culture in schools. My hypothesis is that when there is a lack of clear purpose, leaders' efforts have to be focused on the downstream, noticing those that have fallen in and scrambling to hoist them out.

Looking back, the carefully sequenced knowledge and understanding that we want for children was nowhere near the standard that exists now. Collectively, we have a much better understanding of curriculum design than we did then. Back then, the result of this retrospective gaping hole was a focus on assessment, on checking; high stakes testing, lesson observations and work scrutinies.

A well defined, communicated and understood purpose is important because of the role it plays in Page 1 Article Archive -- Education & Leadership school life. It contributes to the climate (how it feels to work at this school) and in turn what colleagues do with the short time that they have available to influence what children think about and ultimately learn.
There is certainly scope for more quality assuring further upstream though, scrutinising our purpose so that we can get it right, stopping people falling in in the first place." Page 2
